newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian rights body suggests riot compensation.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian rights body suggests riot compensation.

text.p: Indonesia's official National Commission on Human Rights said on Wednesday the government should consider compensating victims of riots last month in which 24 churches were burned.
In an official report on the October 10 incident in the town of Situbondo in East Java province, the commission confirmed the death toll of five and gave a list of the material damage.

The report obtained by Reuters said 24 churches, a temple, six Catholic schools, five priests' houses, six shops, a courthouse and an orphanage were burnt in the town 160 km (100 miles) east of Indonesia's second-largest city, Surabaya.
Nine cars and three motorbikes were also burnt, it said.

"The commission recommends...the government consider giving compensation or assistance to the victims or families of victims whose rights were violated," the report, co-signed by chairman Munawir Sjadzali and secretary-general Baharuddin Lopa, said.
Arnold Baramuli, a member of the commission's fact-finding team into the incident, had said on Tuesday the attacks were not a religious problem.
"It is not a problem between religions. It is purely a criminal matter," Baramuli said while leaving a commission meeting that had been considering the report and other matters.
However, the official report said the incident started after a crowd was dissatisfied with the sentence asked for by prosecutors in a blasphemy trial of a Moslem heretic in Situbondo on October 10.

"From the events in Situbondo it appears there are still complex problems in the community, including the relationship between religions that need to be examined closer and overcome," the report said.
"This needs to be done to end the atmosphere of suspicion and caution."
Police said last week 54 of the 145 people detained after the riot would soon be taken to court.
Religious discord is a sensitive problem in Indonesia, where about 85 percent of the country's 196 million people are followers of Islam.
The state ideology Pancasila promotes tolerance and the government recognises the five major religions of Islam, Catholicism, Protestantism, Hinduism and Buddhism.
